es.summary: El ERGE es la regurgitación crónica de contenido gástrico al esófago por incompetencia del esfínter esofágico inferior, provocando irritación y síntomas típicos.
key_points: Incompetencia del esfínter esofágico inferior permite el reflujo ácido.
Factores de riesgo: obesidad, embarazo, tabaquismo y hernia hiatal.
Síntomas principales: pirosis, regurgitación y dolor torácico retroesternal.
Complicaciones: esofagitis erosiva, esófago de Barrett y estenosis.
Tratamiento de primera línea: cambios de estilo de vida y inhibidores de la bomba de protones.

pathophysiology: El esfínter esofágico inferior (EEI) pierde tono o se relaja inadecuadamente.
El contenido ácido del estómago retrocede al esófago.
El ácido daña la mucosa escamosa, desencadenando inflamación y reparación crónica.
risk_factors: Embarazo por aumento de presión intraabdominal.
Tabaquismo y exposición a humo de segunda mano.
Consumo frecuente de alimentos grasos, chocolate, cafeína, alcohol y menta.
signs_symptoms: Pirosis (ardor retroesternal) después de comer o al acostarse.
Regurgitación de contenido ácido al nivel de la faringe.
Dolor torácico que puede confundirse con angina.
Disfagia o odinofagia en casos de esofagitis.
Tos crónica, ronquera y sensación de cuerpo extraño en la garganta.
diagnostics: Endoscopia digestiva alta: erosiones, esófago de Barrett o estenosis.
pH-metría esofágica de 24 h: pH < 4 > 4 % del tiempo es diagnóstico.
Radiografía con bario: puede mostrar reflujo y hernia hiatal.
treatment: Modificaciones de estilo de vida: elevar cabecera 15‑20 cm, evitar comidas 2‑3 h antes de acostarse.
Inhibidores de la bomba de protones (omeprazol, esomeprazol).
Antagonistas H2 (ranitidina, famotidina) para casos leves.
Antiácidos (hidróxido de aluminio/magnesio) para alivio rápido.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia e intensidad de pirosis y regurgitación.
Monitorear signos de aspiración: tos, cambios en auscultación pulmonar.
Registrar peso y patrón de alimentación.
Enseñar posición semisentada después de comer y uso de almohada elevadora.
Reforzar adherencia a medicación y cambios dietéticos.
patient_teaching: Evitar comidas copiosas, grasas, chocolate, cafeína y alcohol.
No acostarse ≤ 2 h después de comer; elevar la cabecera de la cama.
Mantener peso corporal adecuado; ejercicio regular.
No fumar y evitar exposición a humo de segunda mano.
Tomar los inhibidores de bomba de protones según indicación, sin interrumpir sin consultar.

outcomes: NOC: Mantener vía aérea libre de aspiración – No presenta tos ni cambios en auscultación pulmonar en 48 h.
NOC: Reducción de episodios de tos nocturna – ≤ 1 episodio por semana al final de la semana de cuidados.

interventions.action: Colocar al paciente en posición semisentada (30‑45°) después de cada comida
interventions.rationale: Reduce el reflujo y el riesgo de que el contenido gástrico sea aspirado.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de aspiración cada 4 h (tos, sibilancias, cambios en saturación)
interventions.rationale: Permite detección temprana y respuesta oportuna.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de deglución segura y evitar beber grandes volúmenes de líquido durante las comidas
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la probabilidad de que el contenido regurgite y sea aspirado.

interventions.action: Administrar antiácidos o inhibidores de bomba de protones según prescripción antes de la alimentación
interventions.rationale: Reduce la acidez del contenido gástrico, disminuyendo daño pulmonar si ocurre aspiración.

interventions.action: Mantener la cabecera de la cama elevada 15‑20 cm durante la noche
interventions.rationale: Previene el reflujo nocturno y la aspiración mientras el paciente está acostado.

evidenced_by: disminución de la tolerancia al ejercicio
dolor torácico o ardor después de caminar
outcomes: NOC: Aumentar tolerancia a la actividad – Caminar 30 min sin síntomas de pirosis al cabo de 2 semanas.
NOC: Mejorar nivel de energía – Reporta nivel de energía ≥ 7/10 en escala de valoración en 1 semana.

interventions.action: Planificar actividades en intervalos cortos con descansos frecuentes
interventions.rationale: Permite al paciente acumular actividad sin desencadenar síntomas de reflujo.

interventions.action: Enseñar técnicas de respiración diafragmática durante el ejercicio
interventions.rationale: Reduce la presión intraabdominal y el riesgo de reflujo.

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales y nivel de dolor antes y después de la actividad
interventions.rationale: Detecta intolerancia temprana y evita exacerbación.

interventions.action: Reforzar el uso de medicación antiácida antes de la actividad física programada
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la acidez gástrica durante el esfuerzo.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de evitar comidas copiosas 2 h antes del ejercicio
interventions.rationale: Previene el aumento del contenido gástrico que favorece el reflujo durante la actividad.

en.summary: GERD is chronic regurgitation of gastric contents into the esophagus due to lower esophageal sphincter incompetence, causing irritation and typical symptoms.
key_points: Lower esophageal sphincter incompetence allows acid reflux.
Risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, smoking, and hiatal hernia.
Primary symptoms: heartburn, regurgitation, and retrosternal chest pain.
Complications: erosive esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, and stenosis.
First‑line treatment: lifestyle changes and proton pump inhibitors.

pathophysiology: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) loses tone or relaxes inappropriately.
Acidic gastric content flows back into the esophagus.
Acid damages the squamous mucosa, triggering inflammation and chronic repair.
risk_factors: Pregnancy due to increased intraabdominal pressure.
Smoking and exposure to second‑hand smoke.
Frequent consumption of fatty foods, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, and mint.
signs_symptoms: Heartburn (retrosternal burning) after meals or when lying down.
Regurgitation of acidic content to the pharynx.
Chest pain that may be mistaken for angina.
Dysphagia or odynophagia in cases of esophagitis.
Chronic cough, hoarseness, and sensation of a foreign body in the throat.
diagnostics: Upper endoscopy: erosions, Barrett’s esophagus, or stenosis.
24‑hour esophageal pH monitoring: pH < 4 > 4 % of the time is diagnostic.
Barium swallow X‑ray: may show reflux and hiatal hernia.
treatment: Lifestyle modifications: elevate head of bed 15‑20 cm, avoid meals 2‑3 h before bedtime.
H2 antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) for mild cases.
nursing_care: Assess frequency and intensity of heartburn and regurgitation.
Monitor for aspiration signs: cough, changes in lung auscultation.
Teach semi‑upright position after meals and use of an elevating pillow.
Reinforce medication adherence and dietary changes.
patient_teaching: Avoid large, fatty meals, chocolate, caffeine, and alcohol.
Do not lie down ≤ 2 h after eating; elevate the bed head.
Maintain a healthy body weight; exercise regularly.
Do not smoke and avoid second‑hand smoke exposure.
Take proton pump inhibitors as prescribed, do not discontinue without consulting.

outcomes: NOC: Maintain airway free of aspiration – No cough or changes in lung auscultation in 48 h.
NOC: Reduce nocturnal cough episodes – ≤ 1 episode per week by end of care week.

interventions.action: Place patient in semi‑upright position (30‑45°) after each meal
interventions.rationale: Reduces reflux and the risk of gastric content being aspirated.

interventions.action: Assess aspiration signs every 4 h (cough, wheeze, saturation changes)
interventions.rationale: Allows early detection and timely response.

interventions.action: Teach patient safe swallowing techniques and avoid large volumes of liquid during meals
interventions.rationale: Decreases likelihood of regurgitation and aspiration.

interventions.action: Administer antacids or proton pump inhibitors as prescribed before meals
interventions.rationale: Reduces gastric acidity, decreasing lung injury if aspiration occurs.

interventions.action: Keep head of bed elevated 15‑20 cm during the night
interventions.rationale: Prevents nocturnal reflux and aspiration while patient is supine.

evidenced_by: chest pain or burning after walking
outcomes: NOC: Increase activity tolerance – Walk 30 min without heartburn symptoms after 2 weeks.
NOC: Improve energy level – Report energy level ≥ 7/10 on assessment scale in 1 week.

interventions.action: Plan activities in short intervals with frequent rest breaks
interventions.rationale: Allows patient to accumulate activity without triggering reflux symptoms.

interventions.action: Teach diaphragmatic breathing techniques during exercise
interventions.rationale: Reduces intraabdominal pressure and reflux risk.

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and pain level before and after activity
interventions.rationale: Detects early intolerance and prevents exacerbation.

interventions.action: Reinforce use of antacid medication before scheduled physical activity
interventions.rationale: Decreases gastric acidity during exertion.

interventions.action: Educate patient on importance of avoiding large meals 2 h before exercise
interventions.rationale: Prevents increased gastric content that promotes reflux during activity.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: GERD can happen when the muscle at the bottom of your esophagus becomes weak or relaxes at the wrong time.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: Stomach contents can then move back up and irritate the esophagus.

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: researchers believe that damage to the squamous esophageal cells resulting from gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) causes the cells to undergo constant repair and wound healing.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: You are more likely to have GERD if you: Are overweight or have obesity Are pregnant Smoke or are around secondhand smoke Have a hiatal hernia (when part of the stomach pushes up into the chest)

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Have a hiatal hernia (when part of the stomach pushes up into the chest)

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: In some cases, Barrett’s esophagus can cause ulceration and stricture, and patients may have the symptoms of dysphagia or odynophagia (painful swallowing).

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD): Chronic acid reflux, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) can lead to irritation of the throat, causing hoarseness, cough, and throat discomfort.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: An upper endoscopy will confirm visual changes to the tissues in the esophagus.

sections.diagnostics.3.quote: An upper GI series, or barium swallow, can check for GERD, dysphagia , hiatal hernia, ulcers, tumors, or achalasia.

sections.complications.0.quote: Raberprazole GERD Peptic and esophageal ulcers Erosive esophagitis H. pylori infection Zollinger-Ellison syndrome May cause kidney damage Can interfere with the liver metabolism of other drugs Long-term therapy can cause hypomagnesemia.

sections.complications.4.quote: The cells that develop on the esophagus can be precancerous and increase the patient’s chance of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma (Souza & Spechler, 2022).

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: The nurse inquires about the frequency, severity, and duration of symptoms, and if symptoms interrupt the patient’s sleep.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Symptom improvement and patient understanding of the importance of diet modification and medication adherence are the goals of treatment for Barrett’s esophagus .

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Foods that are spicy, fatty, acidic, or contain caffeine, carbonation, or alcohol can exacerbate symptoms of reflux and heartburn and trigger episodes of odynophagia or dysphagia.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Lifestyle changes can include: Eating smaller meals and avoiding lying down for at least 2-3 hours after eating Avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, such as spicy foods, chocolate, caffeine, or fatty foods Losing weight if needed Raising the head of your bed Quitting smoking
